question: What is the primary purpose of incineration in healthcare waste management?

options.A: To recycle plastics into new medical equipment
options.B: To reduce waste volume and completely destroy pathogens through high temperatures
options.C: To convert medical waste into safe drinking water
options.D: To store radioactive materials underground

explanation: Incineration uses high temperatures to destroy pathogens and significantly reduce the volume and weight of combustible medical waste. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h4)

question: What dangerous pollutants can be emitted by poorly maintained or traditional incinerators?

options.A: Oxygen and nitrogen gas
options.B: Dioxins, furans, and heavy metals
options.C: Pure water vapor and carbon
options.D: Vitamin aerosols

explanation: Incomplete combustion in poor incinerators releases toxic substances like dioxins, furans, and heavy metals, harming the environment and public health. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h4)

question: How does an autoclave sterilize infectious healthcare waste?

options.A: By utilizing chemical bleaching agents soaked for 48 hours
options.B: By using moist heat in the form of pressurized steam
options.C: By freezing waste to sub-zero temperatures
options.D: By exposing waste to direct open sunlight

explanation: Autoclaves use moist heat under high pressure to effectively destroy pathogens and sterilize infectious waste. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h5)

question: What is a major environmental advantage of non-incineration technologies like autoclaving?

options.A: They generate massive amounts of electricity
options.B: They produce toxic ash that fertilizes soil
options.C: They do not emit harmful air pollutants like dioxins and furans
options.D: They eliminate the need for any waste sorting

explanation: Non-incineration technologies avoid burning materials, thereby eliminating the release of toxic air emissions such as dioxins and furans. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h5)

question: What is the primary function of encapsulation in healthcare waste management?

options.A: To dissolve plastics into clear liquid fertilizer
options.B: To immobilize waste such as pharmaceuticals or sharps inside a solid matrix like cement
options.C: To vaporize infectious microorganisms using high-frequency sound waves
options.D: To bleach general waste white for municipal recycling

explanation: Encapsulation involves sealing waste inside a container with a solidifying agent like cement to prevent leaching and unauthorized retrieval. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h6)

question: What factor is critical for the success of chemical disinfection of healthcare waste?

options.A: Storing the waste in a dark, cold refrigerator
options.B: Ensuring adequate contact time and proper chemical concentration
options.C: Mixing the waste with household food scraps
options.D: Exposing the chemical container to open flame

explanation: Chemical disinfection relies heavily on correct chemical concentration and sufficient contact time to ensure all pathogens are successfully destroyed. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h6)

question: Why is the practice of recapping needles generally discouraged?

options.A: It dulls the sharp tip of the needle
options.B: It increases the risk of accidental needle-stick injuries
options.C: It violates hospital financial policies
options.D: It causes the syringe to leak medication

explanation: Most accidental needle-stick injuries happen when healthcare workers attempt to recap used needles after a procedure. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h7)

question: At what capacity should a sharps safety box be securely closed and replaced?

options.A: When it is 25% full
options.B: When it is completely overflowing
options.C: When it reaches approximately 75% full
options.D: Only at the end of every calendar month

explanation: Safety boxes should be sealed and replaced when they reach 75% capacity to prevent accidental punctures or overflows. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h7)

question: What key engineering feature distinguishes a sanitary landfill from an open dump?

options.A: Open burning of waste every evening
options.B: Impermeable bottom liners and leachate collection systems
options.C: Unrestricted access for local scavengers and stray animals
options.D: Lack of any soil covering or regulatory oversight

explanation: Sanitary landfills are engineered with impermeable liners and leachate collection systems to protect groundwater and the environment from contamination. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h8)

question: Under what condition can healthcare waste be integrated with municipal solid waste for final disposal?

options.A: When it has been thoroughly treated, rendered non-hazardous, and made unrecognizable
options.B: Whenever the hospital run out of yellow biohazard bags
options.C: If the waste contains untreated sharp needles
options.D: Only when disposed of during nighttime hours

explanation: Only waste that has undergone complete treatment (like autoclaving and shredding) to remove its hazardous and recognizable nature can be integrated with municipal waste. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h8)

question: To whom do standard precautions apply in a healthcare setting?

options.A: Only to patients diagnosed with known contagious diseases
options.B: To all patients regardless of their diagnosis or infection status
options.C: Only to surgical patients in the operating theater
options.D: Only to housekeeping and waste management staff

explanation: Standard precautions are universal infection control measures applied to the care of all patients, regardless of their suspected or confirmed infection status. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h9)

question: What is an essential component of institutional occupational safety for healthcare workers managing waste?

options.A: Mandatory Hepatitis B vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis protocols
options.B: Prohibition of wearing any form of gloves during cleaning
options.C: Encouraging staff to recap needles rapidly with two hands
options.D: Eliminating hand hygiene stations to save hospital water

explanation: Providing immunizations like Hepatitis B vaccine and clear post-exposure prophylaxis protocols are vital occupational health safeguards for staff handling medical waste. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h9)

question: Which Nigerian agency is prominently involved in enforcing environmental standards and regulations regarding waste?

options.A: National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA)
options.B: National Football Federation (NFF)
options.C: Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA)
options.D: Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC)

explanation: NESREA is a key federal agency responsible for setting and enforcing environmental standards and regulations, including hazardous waste management in Nigeria. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h10)

question: What is a major requirement for healthcare institutions under national health care waste management policies?

options.A: Outsourcing all nursing care to foreign agencies
options.B: Developing site-specific Health Care Waste Management Plans and conducting staff training
options.C: Burning all waste openly in hospital parking lots
options.D: Mixing hazardous materials with household garbage

explanation: National policies require healthcare facilities to establish formal waste management plans, provide training, and ensure strict auditing of their waste processes. [learn more](GST114_U6_T13#GST114_U6_T13_h10)

question: Which of the following best defines a parasite in medical parasitology?

options.A: An organism that lives independently and benefits its host mutually
options.B: An organism that lives on or within a host, deriving nourishment while causing harm
options.C: A free-living organism that shares a commensal relationship with humans
options.D: An environmental bacterium that decomposes organic matter

explanation: A parasite is specifically defined as an organism that lives on or within another living organism (the host) and obtains nourishment from it while causing harm or providing no benefit. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h1)

question: Why is the study of parasitology particularly crucial for nursing students practicing in Nigeria?

options.A: Parasitic infections are completely eradicated in the region
options.B: It focuses solely on viral genetics and mutating strains
options.C: Parasitic infections remain a major public health challenge affecting vulnerable groups
options.D: It replaces the need for pharmacology and surgical nursing

explanation: Understanding parasitology is vital in Nigeria because parasitic infections are a major public health concern, causing significant illness especially in vulnerable populations like children and pregnant women. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h1)

question: In which type of host does a parasite reach sexual maturity and reproduce sexually?

options.A: Intermediate host
options.B: Reservoir host
options.C: Definitive host
options.D: Vector host

explanation: The definitive host is the specific organism in which the parasite attains sexual maturity and undergoes sexual reproduction. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h2)

question: How are endoparasites distinguished from ectoparasites?

options.A: Endoparasites live inside the host's body, whereas ectoparasites live on the external surface
options.B: Endoparasites only affect animals, while ectoparasites only affect humans
options.C: Endoparasites are always unicellular protozoa, whereas ectoparasites are multicellular worms
options.D: Endoparasites do not require a host to complete their life cycle

explanation: Endoparasites reside internally within tissues or organs of the host, while ectoparasites inhabit the outer surface or skin of the host. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h2)

question: Which of the following groups represents microscopic, single-celled eukaryotic parasites?

options.A: Nematodes
options.B: Cestodes
options.C: Protozoa
options.D: Trematodes

explanation: Protozoa are microscopic, single-celled eukaryotic organisms capable of multiplying inside the human host, unlike multicellular helminths. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h3)

question: Ascaris lumbricoides and hookworms belong to which major class of helminths?

options.A: Cestodes
options.B: Trematodes
options.C: Nematodes
options.D: Sporozoans

explanation: Nematodes are roundworms, which include common intestinal parasites such as Ascaris lumbricoides and hookworms. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h3)

question: What characterizes a direct parasitic life cycle?

options.A: It requires at least three different intermediate animal hosts
options.B: It requires only a single definitive host without needing an intermediate host
options.C: It is exclusively transmitted through mosquito bites
options.D: It can only be completed inside the vector's salivary glands

explanation: A direct life cycle means the parasite requires only one definitive host to complete its life cycle, typically spreading through contaminated soil or water. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h4)

question: How do Schistosoma species commonly gain entry into the human body?

options.A: Active skin penetration of cercariae from contaminated fresh water
options.B: Inhalation of airborne respiratory droplets
options.C: Bites from infected blackflies
options.D: Ingestion of poorly cooked beef

explanation: Schistosoma larvae (cercariae) are released from freshwater snails and actively penetrate human skin when individuals wade or swim in contaminated water. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h4)

question: Which of the following is a primary mechanism of pathogenesis in heavy Ascaris lumbricoides infections?

options.A: Destruction of red blood cells in the spleen
options.B: Mechanical obstruction of intestinal lumen or ducts
options.C: Neurotoxin production leading to instant paralysis
options.D: Invasion of the central nervous system neurons

explanation: Large numbers of Ascaris worms can cause physical crowding, leading to mechanical obstruction of the intestinal lumen or biliary ducts. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h5)

question: Which antibody class is typically elevated during helminthic parasite infections as part of the host immune response?

options.A: IgD
options.B: IgG
options.C: IgE
options.D: IgM

explanation: IgE antibodies and eosinophils play a major protective role and elevate significantly during helminth (worm) infections. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary laboratory method used for diagnosing blood-borne parasitic infections like malaria?

options.A: Stool culture and sensitivity
options.B: Thick and thin blood smears examined microscopically
options.C: Sputum acid-fast staining
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid viral titer

explanation: Microscopic examination of thick and thin blood smears stained with Giemsa is the gold standard for diagnosing hemoparasites such as Plasmodium species. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h6)

question: Why might a patient with a parasitic infection present with non-specific symptoms or even remain asymptomatic?

options.A: Parasites only infect non-living biological tissues
options.B: Symptoms depend on parasite load, organ involvement, and host immunity
options.C: All parasites instantly destroy the host immune system
options.D: Asymptomatic cases only occur in laboratory animals

explanation: Clinical manifestations vary widely because mild worm burdens or strong host immunity can keep infections asymptomatic, while heavy loads cause severe disease. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h6)

question: Which category of medications is primarily used in the treatment of intestinal worm infections?

options.A: Anthelmintics
options.B: Antivirals
options.C: Antifungals
options.D: Bronchodilators

explanation: Anthelmintics are specialized medications used to treat infections caused by parasitic worms (helminths), such as albendazole and mebendazole. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h7)

question: What is an essential component of community-level prevention for vector-borne parasitic infections like malaria?

options.A: Mass administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets and clearing stagnant water
options.C: Mandatory isolation of all infected patients in hospital wards
options.D: Complete dietary restriction of protein intake

explanation: Vector control, including sleeping under insecticide-treated nets and eliminating mosquito breeding sites (stagnant water), is vital for preventing vector-borne parasites. [learn more](GST114_U6_T2#GST114_U6_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary role of environmental sanitation in public health nursing?

options.A: To beautify local communities
options.B: To interfere with factors affecting human health and prevent disease transmission
options.C: To replace the need for clinical medications
options.D: To increase hospital admission rates

explanation: Environmental sanitation involves control measures that target physical, biological, and social factors to interrupt the chain of infection and prevent disease transmission. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h1)

question: Which of the following represents a foundational pillar of environmental health?

options.A: High-cost surgical interventions
options.B: Safe water supply and proper excreta disposal
options.C: Intravenous fluid manufacturing
options.D: Private hospital administration

explanation: Safe water supply, proper excreta disposal, solid waste management, and vector control are the core foundational pillars of environmental health. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h1)

question: Which demographic group is particularly vulnerable to the effects of parasitic infections in Nigeria?

options.A: Retired civil servants
options.B: School-aged children
options.C: Urban corporate executives
options.D: Adolescent males in boarding schools

explanation: School-age children are particularly vulnerable, frequently suffering from chronic infections that impair their growth and cognitive development. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h2)

question: Parasitic infections in Nigeria are broadly categorized into which two main groups?

options.A: Bacteria and viruses
options.B: Fungi and prions
options.C: Protozoa and helminths
options.D: Algae and lichens

explanation: Parasitic infections are primarily classified into protozoa (single-celled organisms) and helminths (worms). [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h2)

question: How are hookworm infections typically transmitted to humans from the environment?

options.A: Through the bite of infected mosquitoes
options.B: Through direct skin penetration from contaminated soil
options.C: By drinking boiled water
options.D: Through droplet inhalation

explanation: Hookworms are soil-transmitted helminths whose larvae can directly penetrate the skin of individuals walking barefoot on contaminated soil. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission for water-borne protozoan parasites like Giardia lamblia?

options.A: The fecal-oral route via contaminated water or food
options.B: Direct skin contact with freshwater snails
options.C: Airborne transmission in crowded rooms
options.D: Blood transfusion from an infected donor

explanation: Protozoan parasites like Giardia spread primarily through the fecal-oral route when people consume water or food contaminated with cysts. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h3)

question: What phenomenon occurs when a patient is treated medically but returns with the same infection due to unimproved living conditions?

options.A: Drug resistance
options.B: Revolving-door syndrome of repeated infections
options.C: Chronic immunosuppression
options.D: Anaphylactic shock

explanation: Treating a patient without fixing their unsanitary environment leads to repeated reinfections, often described as a revolving-door syndrome of hospital admissions. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h4)

question: How do houseflies contribute to disease spread in areas with poor sanitation?

options.A: By biting humans to transmit malaria
options.B: By acting as mechanical vectors transferring pathogens from feces to food
options.C: By contaminating groundwater supplies with urine
options.D: By destroying agricultural crops

explanation: Flies act as mechanical vectors, picking up pathogens from exposed feces and depositing them onto unprotected food items. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h4)

question: Which clinical manifestation is most characteristic of a severe chronic hookworm infection?

options.A: Jaundice and dark urine
options.B: Iron-deficiency anemia and pallor
options.C: Blood in the stool accompanied by high fever
options.D: Skin rashes and localized pruritus

explanation: Severe hookworm infections cause chronic intestinal blood loss, leading directly to iron-deficiency anemia, pallor, and fatigue. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h5)

question: What is a key nursing action during the assessment of a patient suspected of having a parasitic infection?

options.A: Prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately
options.B: Taking a detailed history regarding living and sanitary conditions
options.C: Performing emergency surgical intervention
options.D: Restricting all fluid intake for 24 hours

explanation: A thorough patient assessment requires taking detailed travel, dietary, and living condition histories to identify potential exposure sources. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h5)

question: Which medication class is standard for treating soil-transmitted helminths like Ascaris?

options.A: Antihelmintics such as albendazole
options.B: Broad-spectrum antivirals
options.C: Inhaled bronchodilators
options.D: Topical antifungal creams

explanation: Antihelmintic medications like albendazole and mebendazole are the standard pharmacological treatments for soil-transmitted helminths. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h6)

question: What is an essential nursing responsibility during pharmacological treatment of parasitic infections?

options.A: Stopping medication as soon as symptoms subside
options.B: Ensuring correct dosage and monitoring for adverse drug reactions
options.C: Administering drugs exclusively via the intravenous route
options.D: Avoiding patient education to prevent confusion

explanation: Nurses must ensure correct medication administration, observe for adverse reactions, and educate patients on completing their full regimen. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h6)

question: What is considered one of the most cost-effective measures against parasitic infections?

options.A: Constructing tertiary intensive care units
options.B: Community health education and environmental sanitation
options.C: Routinely prescribing prophylactic antibiotics to entire cities
options.D: Importing expensive foreign medical equipment

explanation: Community health education and environmental sanitation are sustainable, cost-effective strategies for preventing the spread of parasites. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h7)

question: Which behavior should community health nurses actively promote to prevent water and food-borne parasites?

options.A: Walking barefoot in agricultural fields
options.B: Handwashing with soap after using the toilet and before eating
options.C: Consuming untreated surface water directly from streams
options.D: Leaving household waste uncovered in living areas

explanation: Proper handwashing with soap after using the toilet and before handling food is a primary hygiene behavior that prevents fecal-oral transmission. [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary public health consequence of inadequately managed sewage disposal?

options.A: Increased agricultural crop yields
options.B: The rapid spread of waterborne diseases
options.C: Enhancement of municipal water supplies
options.D: Reduction of industrial chemical pollution

explanation: Inadequately managed sewage often contaminates local water sources and living environments, which directly facilitates the rapid spread of waterborne diseases. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h1)

question: Why is the study of sewage disposal particularly important for student nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: To design municipal wastewater treatment plants
options.B: To enforce environmental sanitation fines
options.C: To understand disease transmission and promote community hygiene
options.D: To manufacture chemical disinfectants

explanation: Understanding sewage disposal helps nurses comprehend disease transmission cycles so they can effectively educate the public and promote community hygiene. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h1)

question: What percentage of raw sewage typically consists of water?

options.A: Approximately 50%
options.B: Approximately 75%
options.C: Approximately 90%
options.D: Approximately 99.9%

explanation: Raw sewage is overwhelmingly liquid, with water typically making up about 99.9% of its total composition. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following describes the microbiological nature of raw sewage?

options.A: It is completely sterile
options.B: It is a dense ecosystem teeming with bacteria, viruses, and parasites
options.C: It contains only harmless plant fungi
options.D: It lacks any living microorganisms

explanation: Raw sewage is a dense microbiological ecosystem containing numerous bacteria, viruses, and parasites shed by human populations. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h2)

question: What is the primary transmission route for pathogens found in improperly disposed sewage?

options.A: Airborne droplet inhalation
options.B: Direct skin contact with healthy skin
options.C: The fecal-oral route via contaminated water or food
options.D: Insect bites from mosquitoes

explanation: Pathogens from sewage typically enter new hosts via the fecal-oral route through contaminated drinking water, recreational water, or food. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which of the following bacterial diseases is classically associated with sewage-contaminated water sources?

options.A: Cholera
options.B: Tuberculosis
options.C: Malaria
options.D: Tetanus

explanation: Cholera is a severe waterborne bacterial disease caused by Vibrio cholerae, often spreading rapidly through contaminated water supplies. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary function of a septic tank in an on-site sewage disposal system?

options.A: To incinerate all solid waste completely
options.B: To allow sedimentation and anaerobic digestion of wastewater solids
options.C: To pump drinking water into households
options.D: To chemically purify water for immediate consumption

explanation: A septic tank receives wastewater to allow heavy solids to settle as sludge and lighter materials to form scum through anaerobic digestion. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h4)

question: What happens to the liquid effluent after it leaves a septic tank?

options.A: It is piped directly into municipal swimming pools
options.B: It flows into a drain field for natural soil filtration
options.C: It is boiled and bottled for commercial sale
options.D: It is sprayed into the atmosphere to evaporate

explanation: Effluent flows from the septic tank into a drain field, where it filters through the soil which acts as a natural biological filter. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary force that drives wastewater flow through standard municipal sewer pipes?

options.A: Solar power
options.B: High-pressure air pumps
options.C: Gravity along sloped pipes
options.D: Manual dredging

explanation: Standard municipal sewer pipes are engineered with a slope so that gravity can naturally drive the flow of wastewater. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h5)

question: What is a major challenge facing off-site municipal sewage systems in rapidly growing urban areas?

options.A: An excess of trained plumbing engineers
options.B: Aging infrastructure and sewer overflows due to population growth
options.C: Too little wastewater being generated
options.D: The freezing of underground pipes

explanation: Rapid population growth combined with aging infrastructure often leads to blockages, sewer overflows, and untreated discharges in urban areas. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h5)

question: Which stage of wastewater treatment primarily relies on physical screening and sedimentation to remove large debris and settleable solids?

options.A: Primary treatment
options.B: Secondary treatment
options.C: Tertiary treatment
options.D: Quaternary distillation

explanation: Primary treatment is a physical process that uses screens and sedimentation tanks to remove large debris and heavy settleable solids. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of secondary wastewater treatment?

options.A: To add heavy metals back into the water
options.B: To use aerobic microorganisms to break down dissolved and suspended organic matter
options.C: To freeze the wastewater into solid blocks
options.D: To filter out visible plastic bottles

explanation: Secondary treatment utilizes aerobic microorganisms in aeration tanks or trickling filters to consume and break down organic pollutants. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h6)

question: What is the effect of high biological oxygen demand (BOD) caused by sewage pollution in a river?

options.A: It increases the amount of dissolved oxygen for fish
options.B: It causes severe oxygen depletion, leading to fish kills and hypoxia
options.C: It purifies the water instantly
options.D: It freezes the river surface

explanation: High BOD means microorganisms use up available oxygen to break down waste, leading to severe oxygen depletion (hypoxia) and fish kills. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h7)

question: What phenomenon is triggered when nitrogen and phosphorus from sewage enter aquatic ecosystems?

options.A: Desertification
options.B: Eutrophication and explosive algal blooms
options.C: Salinization of freshwater
options.D: Tectonic plate shifts

explanation: Nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus from sewage cause eutrophication, which results in massive algal blooms that suffocate aquatic life. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h7)

question: What is a key clinical and community responsibility of a nurse during a suspected waterborne disease outbreak?

options.A: Building concrete sewage treatment plants single-handedly
options.B: Identifying disease clusters and promptly reporting them to public health authorities
options.C: Isolating the entire town permanently
options.D: Prescribing antibiotics without a medical diagnosis

explanation: Nurses perform epidemiological surveillance by identifying disease clusters and reporting them quickly to help prevent a full-scale epidemic. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h8)

question: How do nurses contribute to disease prevention at the grassroots community level?

options.A: By educating households on handwashing, safe water storage, and sanitary latrines
options.B: By taxing residents who fail to clean their streets
options.C: By engineering underground drainage pipes
options.D: By manufacturing chemical water purifiers

explanation: Nurses educate communities on hygiene practices like handwashing, safe water storage, and proper sanitation to prevent illness. [learn more](GST114_U6_T4#GST114_U6_T4_h8)

question: Why is waste considered more than just inert rubbish in healthcare settings?

options.A: It takes up too much physical space in hospitals
options.B: It acts as a dynamic reservoir of infectious microbial populations
options.C: It is always chemically reactive and unstable
options.D: It smells unpleasant to patients and staff

explanation: Healthcare waste harbors diverse pathogens like bacteria and viruses that can multiply rapidly on organic matter, making it an infectious reservoir rather than just inert rubbish. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h1)

question: Which of the following is a key objective of proper waste management in relation to microbiology?

options.A: Increasing the rate of microbial reproduction
options.B: Enhancing the aesthetic appeal of hospital grounds
options.C: Breaking the chain of infection by containing pathogens
options.D: Reducing the cost of hospital administrative supplies

explanation: Proper containment and disposal break the chain of infection, protecting patients, staff, and the community from healthcare-associated infections. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h1)

question: Which of the following best describes general healthcare waste?

options.A: Used surgical scalpels and blades
options.B: Expired chemotherapy medications
options.C: Paper, cardboard, and food leftovers from non-isolated areas
options.D: Human tissues and amputated body parts

explanation: General waste resembles household refuse like paper and food scraps that do not pose special biological hazards. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h2)

question: Why is accurate classification of healthcare waste essential?

options.A: It ensures hazardous waste is treated safely without treating all waste as hazardous
options.B: It allows hospitals to eliminate waste management costs entirely
options.C: It guarantees that all waste can be recycled into domestic goods
options.D: It prevents the generation of municipal garbage

explanation: Proper classification balances safety and cost, ensuring high-risk hazardous materials are managed strictly while avoiding expensive special treatment for safe general refuse. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h2)

question: What is a primary danger associated with improperly disposed sharps?

options.A: Contamination of local groundwater with heavy metals
options.B: Direct inoculation of blood-borne pathogens into the bloodstream
options.C: Attraction of stray animals to hospital premises
options.D: Foul odors affecting patient recovery in wards

explanation: Improperly disposed sharps can cause needlestick injuries, directly inoculating blood-borne pathogens like HIV and Hepatitis into the bloodstream. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h3)

question: How do disease vectors contribute to microbiological risks from poor waste disposal?

options.A: They neutralize harmful bacteria in the soil
options.B: They mechanically transfer pathogens from waste to food and water supplies
options.C: They recycle pharmaceutical waste safely
options.D: They act as natural incinerators for infectious waste

explanation: Vectors like flies and rodents feed on unsecured waste and mechanically transfer pathogens to food and water, causing disease outbreaks. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h3)

question: At what point should healthcare waste segregation take place?

options.A: At the exact point of generation by the clinician
options.B: At the municipal dumping site by waste collectors
options.C: At the end of the shift in the utility room
options.D: After the waste has been compacted in the basement

explanation: Segregation must happen immediately at the point of generation to minimize handling risks and prevent errors. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of using puncture-resistant safety boxes?

options.A: To store confidential patient files securely
options.B: To collect general office stationery and paper
options.C: To safely contain needles, syringes, and sharp blades
options.D: To hold expired liquid pharmaceuticals

explanation: Safety boxes are specifically designed to be puncture-resistant to prevent needlestick injuries from sharps like needles and blades. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h4)

question: What is the maximum capacity to which waste bags should be filled before sealing?

options.A: 100% capacity
options.B: 75% capacity
options.C: 50% capacity
options.D: 90% capacity

explanation: Waste bags and containers should be sealed at three-quarters (75%) capacity to prevent bursting, spilling, or accidental exposure. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h5)

question: How should waste bags be lifted and carried during transport?

options.A: Clutched tightly against the chest for better balance
options.B: Dragged along the floor to reduce arm fatigue
options.C: Lifted by their necks away from the body
options.D: Balanced on the head for easy navigation

explanation: Bags must be lifted by their necks away from the body to protect against punctures from improperly discarded sharps hidden inside. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h5)

question: Which waste treatment technology uses high-pressure steam to destroy all microbial life including spores?

options.A: Incineration
options.B: Autoclaving
options.C: Open burning
options.D: Municipal landfilling

explanation: Autoclaving uses pressurized steam and moist heat to effectively sterilize infectious waste and destroy microbial spores. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h6)

question: What is a primary advantage of modern dual-chamber incineration?

options.A: It converts all plastic waste into reusable medical equipment
options.B: It operates at low temperatures without producing emissions
options.C: It completely destroys pathogens and anatomical waste while reducing volume
options.D: It requires no specialized operator training

explanation: Incineration uses high temperatures to achieve complete thermal destruction of pathogens and anatomical waste while significantly reducing waste volume. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h6)

question: What is the recommended immediate action following an accidental needlestick injury?

options.A: Apply an antiseptic ointment and bandage without washing
options.B: Squeeze the wound tightly to force out all trapped blood
options.C: Wash the site immediately with soap and running water
options.D: Ignore it if the patient appears healthy and asymptomatic

explanation: Washing the injured site immediately with soap and running water helps remove contaminants and reduces the risk of pathogen transmission. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h7)

question: Which vaccination is mandatory for nursing students and clinical staff to prevent occupational blood-borne infections?

options.A: BCG vaccine
options.B: Hepatitis B vaccine
options.C: Tetanus toxoid
options.D: Oral polio vaccine

explanation: Hepatitis B immunization is mandatory for healthcare workers to protect against occupational exposure to blood-borne pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h7)

question: Which Nigerian agency is responsible for enforcing environmental standards and regulations, including medical waste management?

options.A: National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)
options.B: National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA)
options.C: Nigerian Medical Association (NMA)
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN)

explanation: NESREA is the key federal agency tasked with enforcing environmental standards and regulations enforcement across Nigerian facilities. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h8)

question: What is a major challenge affecting medical waste management in some Nigerian healthcare facilities?

options.A: An excess of advanced incinerators in rural clinics
options.B: Erratic electricity supply and infrastructural deficits
options.C: Overabundance of trained sanitation personnel
options.D: Strict over-regulation by international bodies

explanation: Infrastructural deficits and erratic power supply hinder the effective operation of waste treatment technologies like incinerators in Nigerian facilities. [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary definition of water pollution?

options.A: The natural purification of groundwater aquifers
options.B: The contamination of water bodies typically resulting from human activities
options.C: The evaporation of clean water into the atmosphere
options.D: The increase of aquatic plant life due to heavy rainfall

explanation: Water pollution is defined as the contamination of water bodies such as lakes, rivers, and oceans, typically resulting from human activities. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h1)

question: Why is understanding water pollution particularly important for nursing students in Nigeria?

options.A: It helps them design industrial factories
options.B: It is required for marine navigation exams
options.C: It is critical for addressing public health crises and preventing waterborne outbreaks
options.D: It allows them to practice commercial fishing

explanation: Understanding water pollution is vital because contaminated water causes numerous infectious diseases, and nurses need this knowledge to assess health risks and prevent outbreaks. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h1)

question: Which of the following best describes chemical pollutants in water?

options.A: Bacteria and viruses from sewage
options.B: Heavy metals and synthetic pesticides
options.C: Floating plastic bottles and debris
options.D: Dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide

explanation: Chemical pollutants include heavy metals like lead and mercury, as well as synthetic compounds like pesticides and industrial solvents. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h2)

question: What is the direct consequence of nutrient pollution such as excessive nitrogen and phosphorus runoff?

options.A: Increased dissolved oxygen levels
options.B: Eutrophication and algal blooms causing dead zones
options.C: Purification of heavy metal toxins
options.D: Immediate boiling of the water body

explanation: Excessive nutrient runoff leads to eutrophication, causing algal blooms that deplete dissolved oxygen and create dead zones. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h2)

question: What characterizes a point source of water pollution?

options.A: Diffuse runoff from agricultural farmlands
options.B: Discrete, identifiable locations like factory pipes or outfalls
options.C: Widespread urban stormwater runoff
options.D: Rainwater falling directly from the atmosphere

explanation: Point sources are discrete, identifiable conveyances such as pipes or factory outfalls that discharge pollutants directly into water bodies. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of a non-point source of water pollution?

options.A: Treated effluent from a municipal wastewater plant pipe
options.B: Industrial waste discharged from a chemical factory outfall
options.C: Agricultural runoff containing fertilizers and pesticides
options.D: A leaking pipe from an oil refinery

explanation: Agricultural runoff is a non-point source because it involves diffuse, widespread runoff that cannot be traced back to a single discharge point. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following is a protozoan pathogen commonly associated with contaminated water?

options.A: Vibrio cholerae
options.B: Hepatitis A virus
options.C: Giardia lamblia
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Giardia lamblia is a protozoan parasite commonly found in contaminated water sources that causes gastrointestinal illness. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary clinical presentation and major risk of waterborne diseases like cholera?

options.A: Chronic joint pain and muscle stiffness
options.B: Severe watery diarrhea leading to rapid dehydration and shock
options.C: Respiratory failure and chronic coughing
options.D: Skin rashes and severe localized itching

explanation: Waterborne diseases like cholera cause acute gastroenteritis presenting with severe watery diarrhea, which can quickly lead to life-threatening dehydration and shock. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h4)

question: What is biomagnification in the context of water pollution?

options.A: The rapid increase of dissolved oxygen in deep water
options.B: The accumulation and increasing concentration of toxins as they move up the food chain
options.C: The natural growth of aquatic plants during spring
options.D: The filtration of heavy metals by aquatic weeds

explanation: Biomagnification refers to the process where toxin concentrations increase as pollutants move up through higher trophic levels in the food chain. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h5)

question: How does oxygen depletion primarily affect aquatic ecosystems?

options.A: It creates vibrant breeding grounds for fish
options.B: It causes fish and other aquatic organisms to suffocate and die
options.C: It purifies heavy metals from the water
options.D: It increases the population of macroinvertebrates

explanation: Oxygen depletion, caused by organic waste or algal blooms, robs the water of dissolved oxygen, leading to the suffocation and death of aquatic life. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h5)

question: What does a high Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) level in a water sample indicate?

options.A: High levels of pure dissolved oxygen for fish
options.B: High amounts of organic pollution and microbial activity
options.C: Excellent drinking water quality
options.D: Complete absence of biological life

explanation: High BOD levels indicate that there is a large amount of organic matter in the water requiring oxygen for decomposition, signifying heavy pollution. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h6)

question: Why are coliform bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, routinely tested in water quality assessments?

options.A: To measure the exact temperature of the water
options.B: To determine the turbidity and cloudiness
options.C: To signal the presence of faecal contamination
options.D: To evaluate the mineral content and pH balance

explanation: Coliform bacteria and E. coli are used as indicator organisms to signal the presence of faecal contamination in water sources. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary objective of secondary wastewater treatment?

options.A: Filtering out large plastic debris and floating trash
options.B: Using biological processes and bacteria to degrade dissolved organic matter
options.C: Desalination of seawater for agricultural use
options.D: Adding heavy metals to preserve the pipe infrastructure

explanation: Secondary treatment utilizes biological processes, such as activated sludge, to break down and remove dissolved and suspended organic matter. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h7)

question: Which tertiary treatment method is commonly used to destroy remaining pathogens in purified water?

options.A: Gravity screening
options.B: Grit sedimentation
options.C: Ultraviolet radiation or chlorination
options.D: Sand filtration without chemicals

explanation: Disinfection methods such as chlorination, ozonation, or ultraviolet radiation are employed during tertiary treatment to destroy remaining pathogenic microorganisms. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h7)

question: What is a primary clinical nursing intervention for a patient suffering from severe dehydration due to a waterborne infection?

options.A: Administering oral rehydration therapy or intravenous fluids
options.B: Recommending strenuous physical exercise
options.C: Restricting all fluid intake for 48 hours
options.D: Prescribing broad-spectrum industrial solvents

explanation: Managing severe dehydration from waterborne infections requires prompt administration of oral rehydration therapy or intravenous fluids to restore electrolyte balance. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h8)

question: In community outreach, what is a key educational message nurses should share regarding water safety?

options.A: Drinking untreated water directly from rivers builds natural immunity
options.B: Boiling drinking water and storing it in clean, covered containers
options.C: Disposing of chemical waste directly into drainage systems
options.D: Avoiding hand washing to preserve natural skin oils

explanation: Nurses educate communities on safe water practices, including boiling drinking water and storing it properly in clean, covered containers to prevent recontamination. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h8)

question: Which of the following best describes how chemical pollutants can affect airborne pathogens?

options.A: They destroy all microorganisms instantly.
options.B: They can cause oxidative stress or modify surface proteins of pathogens.
options.C: They prevent microbes from entering the atmosphere entirely.
options.D: They turn harmful bacteria into beneficial probiotics.

explanation: Chemical pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides interact with microbes by causing oxidative stress or altering their surface proteins, which can impact their viability and virulence. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h1)

question: Why is understanding the intersection of air pollution and microbiology particularly vital for nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: It helps nurses predict exact weather patterns and rainfall.
options.B: It explains the etiology of escalating respiratory morbidities linked to urban emissions and biomass burning.
options.C: It allows nurses to manufacture chemical pollutants in hospitals.
options.D: It is only relevant for surgical instrument sterilization.

explanation: Recognizing how pollutants interact with microbial ecosystems helps nurses understand the root causes of rising respiratory diseases driven by local urban and industrial activities. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h1)

question: What is the primary characteristic of carbon monoxide that makes it dangerous to human health?

options.A: It has a pungent, foul odor that causes immediate fainting.
options.B: It binds avidly to hemoglobin, thereby reducing oxygen delivery to tissues.
options.C: It transforms into ground-level ozone inside the bloodstream.
options.D: It directly stimulates the production of excess mucus in the bronchioles.

explanation: Carbon monoxide binds strongly to hemoglobin, impairing the blood's capacity to transport oxygen throughout the body. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h2)

question: Which of the following represents a major local source of air pollutants such as particulate matter and carbon monoxide in many Nigerian urban areas?

options.A: Hydroelectric power generation plants
options.B: Extensive use of diesel generators and vehicular emissions from aging fleets
options.C: Widespread use of electric public transportation systems
options.D: Strictly regulated zero-emission industrial zones

explanation: Aging vehicular fleets and heavy dependence on diesel generators are primary contributors to urban air pollution in Nigeria. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h2)

question: What are bioaerosols?

options.A: Synthetic chemical compounds produced exclusively in industrial laboratories
options.B: Airborne particles of biological origin, including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and microbial toxins
options.C: Gaseous emissions generated strictly by burning fossil fuels
options.D: Inert mineral dust particles found only in dry desert regions

explanation: Bioaerosols are defined as airborne particles that originate from biological sources, such as bacteria, fungi, and associated toxins. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h3)

question: How do endotoxins from gram-negative bacteria impact the human respiratory system?

options.A: They act as soothing agents that repair damaged alveolar walls.
options.B: They are potent inducers of airway inflammation and can exacerbate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
options.C: They instantly cure viral pneumonia.
options.D: They have no biological effect once the bacteria are dead.

explanation: Endotoxins strongly stimulate airway inflammation, worsening conditions like COPD even if the source bacteria are non-viable. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h3)

question: Which meteorological factor can cause DNA damage and reduce the viability of certain vegetative bacteria and enveloped viruses?

options.A: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight
options.B: Barometric pressure drops
options.C: High relative humidity levels
options.D: Consistent gentle breezes

explanation: UV radiation from sunlight damages microbial DNA and reduces the survival time of many airborne pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h4)

question: What are the three main phases involved in the atmospheric dispersal of microorganisms?

options.A: Inhalation, digestion, and excretion
options.B: Generation, transport, and deposition
options.C: Condensation, evaporation, and precipitation
options.D: Proliferation, mutation, and eradication

explanation: Microbial dispersal through the air sequentially involves the generation of particles, their atmospheric transport, and their eventual deposition. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h4)

question: How do fine particulate matter (PM2.5) affect the respiratory tract compared to coarse particles?

options.A: PM2.5 particles are completely blocked by the tiny hairs in the nostrils.
options.B: PM2.5 particles penetrate deep into the terminal bronchioles and alveoli.
options.C: PM2.5 particles are immediately dissolved in the saliva.
options.D: PM2.5 particles only affect the pharynx and larynx.

explanation: Due to their small size, fine particles like PM2.5 bypass upper airway defenses and reach the deep lung tissues and alveoli. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h5)

question: What is the consequence of air pollutants impairing the mucociliary escalator?

options.A: Enhanced clearance of all foreign particles from the lungs
options.B: Paralysis or destruction of cilia, leading to reduced clearance of inhaled bioaerosols and increased infection risk
options.C: Immediate regeneration of healthy alveolar tissue
options.D: Permanent cessation of breathing

explanation: Damaging the mucociliary escalator stops the lungs from effectively clearing trapped microbes and debris, promoting secondary infections. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h5)

question: Which diagnostic test is primarily used to assess pulmonary function and detect ventilatory defects in patients exposed to air pollution?

options.A: Spirometry
options.B: Complete blood count
options.C: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
options.D: Urinalysis

explanation: Spirometry measures lung function parameters to identify whether a patient has obstructive or restrictive breathing impairments. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h6)

question: What is the clinical utility of sputum Gram stains and cultures in patients affected by air pollution?

options.A: To measure the exact particle concentration of outdoor PM2.5
options.B: To identify specific bacterial or fungal bioaerosols contributing to secondary respiratory infections
options.C: To calculate the patient's exact blood oxygen saturation
options.D: To visualize lung tissue fibrosis on an X-ray

explanation: Sputum analysis helps pinpoint the exact microbial pathogens responsible for infections secondary to environmental respiratory damage. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h6)

question: What is the recommended initial physical positioning for a patient experiencing acute respiratory distress due to an air pollution-related asthma attack?

options.A: Flat supine position
options.B: Trendelenburg position
options.C: High Fowler's or orthopneic position
options.D: Prone position

explanation: Placing the patient in a high Fowler's or orthopneic position maximizes chest expansion and eases the work of breathing. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h7)

question: Which of the following pharmacological agents is commonly administered by nurses to immediately relieve acute bronchoconstriction?

options.A: Short-acting beta-agonist bronchodilators
options.B: Prophylactic oral antibiotics for viral colds
options.C: Intravenous vasopressors
options.D: Diuretics to remove lung fluid

explanation: Short-acting beta-agonist bronchodilators quickly relax tightened airway smooth muscles, relieving acute bronchospasm. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h7)

question: What is an example of a primary prevention strategy against air pollution?

options.A: Treating a patient with intravenous antibiotics in an ICU
options.B: Enforcing stricter environmental regulations on industrial emissions and promoting cleaner energy sources
options.C: Performing spirometry on an elderly patient with chronic cough
options.D: Providing pulmonary rehabilitation exercises for recovering COPD patients

explanation: Primary prevention aims to stop exposure and pollution at the source by enforcing regulations and adopting cleaner energy alternatives. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h8)

question: What is a key focus of tertiary prevention in the context of air pollution management?

options.A: Stopping industrial factories from ever being built
options.B: Rehabilitating individuals with established chronic respiratory diseases to restore functional capacity
options.C: Measuring the daily air quality index using a satellite
options.D: Vaccinating newborns against routine childhood illnesses

explanation: Tertiary prevention focuses on managing existing chronic conditions through rehabilitation to prevent further decline and improve quality of life. [learn more](GST114_U6_T7#GST114_U6_T7_h8)

question: What is a primary microbiological risk associated with improperly handled health care waste?

options.A: Increased hospital building maintenance costs
options.B: The transmission of pathogenic microorganisms to workers and the community
options.C: Rapid depletion of hospital pharmaceutical supplies
options.D: Enhanced nutritional value of municipal landfill soil

explanation: Improperly handled medical waste harbors pathogens like bacteria and viruses, posing a direct biological threat to anyone exposed to it. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h1)

question: How does poorly managed health care waste affect antimicrobial resistance?

options.A: It neutralizes resistant strains completely
options.B: It has no relationship with drug resistance
options.C: It can contribute to the spread of resistant bacterial strains within the population
options.D: It only affects viral replication rates

explanation: Hospital environments harbor resistant strains, and poorly managed waste serves as a vehicle to spread these resistant bacteria locally. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h1)

question: Which of the following is classified as general health care waste?

options.A: Used surgical scalpels
options.B: Expired chemotherapy drugs
options.C: Food remnants from non-infectious ward areas
options.D: Laboratory cultures of Mycobacterium tuberculosis

explanation: General waste is comparable to domestic waste and includes items like food remnants from non-infectious areas that pose no special biological risk. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h2)

question: Why is proper classification of health care waste necessary?

options.A: It ensures that hazardous waste is treated safely without treating all waste as hazardous unnecessarily
options.B: It allows the hospital to recycle all medical equipment directly
options.C: It completely eliminates the generation of sharps waste
options.D: It reduces the need for personal protective equipment

explanation: Proper classification balances safety and practicality, ensuring dangerous waste gets specialized treatment while avoiding the massive cost of treating all waste as hazardous. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h2)

question: What is the most common route of pathogen transmission from sharp waste to healthcare workers?

options.A: Inhalation of chemical fumes
options.B: Percutaneous injury from needles and lancets
options.C: Ingestion of contaminated water
options.D: Direct skin contact with general paper waste

explanation: Carelessly discarded sharps frequently cause percutaneous injuries, directly inoculating bloodborne pathogens into the worker's bloodstream. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h3)

question: Which group of pathogens is most typically inoculated via sharp injuries in healthcare settings?

options.A: Intestinal parasites
options.B: Bloodborne viruses like HBV, HCV, and HIV
options.C: Respiratory molds
options.D: Skin fungi causing ringworm

explanation: Sharps injuries carry a high risk of transmitting bloodborne viruses such as Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h3)

question: At what point should health care waste segregation take place?

options.A: At the incinerator site outside the hospital
options.B: At the exact point of generation
options.C: During the final municipal transport
options.D: Whenever the waste handler has free time

explanation: Waste must be separated at the point of generation to prevent hidden contamination and protect everyone handling it downstream. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h4)

question: What is the maximum recommended fill level for safety boxes used for sharps disposal?

options.A: Completely packed to the brim
options.B: One-quarter full
options.C: Three-quarters full
options.D: Half full

explanation: Containers should never be overfilled beyond the three-quarter mark to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries during closure and disposal. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h4)

question: How should a full waste bag be safely closed for transport?

options.A: Pressed down firmly by hand to compress the contents
options.B: Tied or sealed using the goose-neck method and handled by the neck
options.C: Left open until it reaches the incinerator
options.D: Pierced with air holes to prevent gas buildup

explanation: Bags should be closed securely using the goose-neck method and held by the neck to avoid punctures and direct contact with waste. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h5)

question: What feature is essential for temporary medical waste storage areas?

options.A: Open-air exposure to sunlight for natural drying
options.B: Proximity to the hospital cafeteria for easy access
options.C: Secure enclosure, good ventilation, and protection from scavengers and vectors
options.D: Unrestricted entry for patients and visitors

explanation: Temporary storage facilities must be secure, well-ventilated, and protected from vectors and unauthorized entry to maintain safety. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary mechanism of action in autoclaving medical waste?

options.A: Chemical cementation
options.B: High-pressure, saturated steam sterilization
options.C: Open-air solar drying
options.D: Freezing at sub-zero temperatures

explanation: Autoclaves use high-pressure, saturated steam to destroy microorganisms and sterilize infectious waste and sharps. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h6)

question: Which treatment method involves mixing pharmaceutical waste with cement and water to prevent leaching?

options.A: Inertization
options.B: Microwaving
options.C: Autoclaving
options.D: Incineration

explanation: Inertization solidifies pharmaceutical waste with cement, lime, and water, creating a solid block that stops toxic drugs from leaching into groundwater. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h6)

question: Why are open dumping and open burning of untreated medical waste prohibited?

options.A: They take up too much physical space on hospital grounds
options.B: They contaminate soil, pollute groundwater, and release carcinogens
options.C: They are too expensive compared to municipal landfills
options.D: They slow down the daily hospital administrative workflow

explanation: Open dumping and burning pollute the environment, contaminate water tables, and release harmful toxins into the air, posing severe health risks. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h7)

question: Where should incinerator ash and treated hazardous waste be deposited?

options.A: In ordinary household garbage bins
options.B: In municipal parks and gardens
options.C: In engineered hazardous waste landfills or dedicated ash pits with protective liners
options.D: Directly into local rivers and streams

explanation: Engineered hazardous waste landfills with liners and leachate systems are required to securely contain treated waste and ash without harming the environment. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h7)

question: What is the very first step a nurse should take immediately following an accidental sharps injury?

options.A: Fill out an incident report form for the hospital board
options.B: Wash the wound immediately with soap and running water
options.C: Apply a tight tourniquet above the injury site
options.D: Wait until the end of the shift to report the exposure

explanation: Immediate first aid after a sharps injury requires washing the affected area thoroughly with soap and running water to reduce pathogen load. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h8)

question: Which vaccination is specifically emphasized as a vital occupational safety measure for nurses handling medical waste?

options.A: Hepatitis B vaccine
options.B: Rabies vaccine
options.C: Yellow fever vaccine
options.D: Cholera vaccine

explanation: Hepatitis B vaccination is essential for healthcare workers due to the persistent risk of bloodborne pathogen transmission from sharps injuries. [learn more](GST114_U6_T8#GST114_U6_T8_h8)

question: What percentage of health care waste is typically classified as hazardous?
explanation: Approximately 75% to 90% of health care waste is general, non-hazardous waste, leaving 10% to 25% as hazardous waste with potential for causing injury or infection. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h1)

question: Why is the proper management of health care waste particularly crucial in clinical environments?

options.A: To reduce administrative paperwork for hospital staff
options.B: To prevent disease transmission and protect patients, workers, and communities
options.C: To lower the cost of purchasing hospital uniforms
options.D: To eliminate the need for general housekeeping services

explanation: Proper waste management prevents biological and physical hazards from harming patients, healthcare workers, and the wider community. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h1)

question: Which of the following best describes pathological waste?

options.A: Expired antibiotic tablets and syrups
options.B: Recognizable human tissues, organs, and body parts
options.C: Discarded chemical solvents and disinfectants
options.D: Used needles and surgical scalpels

explanation: Pathological waste specifically consists of recognizable human tissues, organs, and body parts generated during surgeries and autopsies. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h2)

question: What is the primary reason for segregating health care waste at the point of generation?

options.A: To ensure correct color-coding for aesthetic facility appeal
options.B: To reduce the physical weight of general waste bins
options.C: To allow the application of appropriate treatment and disposal methods for each category
options.D: To simplify the auditing process for hospital financial departments

explanation: Proper segregation ensures that hazardous items receive specialized treatment, preventing dangerous mixing that could contaminate entire waste batches. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h2)

question: Which of the following bloodborne pathogens are of primary concern regarding infectious health care waste?

options.A: HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C
options.B: Malaria parasites and typhoid bacteria
options.C: Tuberculosis and streptococcus
options.D: Cholera and influenza viruses

explanation: HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C are critical bloodborne pathogens transmitted through contaminated medical waste and sharp injuries. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h3)

question: How can pathogens from improperly managed medical waste be indirectly transmitted to the community?

options.A: Through direct inhalation of clean hospital air conditioning
options.B: Via vectors such as rodents, flies, and stray animals scavenging at dumpsites
options.C: By drinking treated municipal tap water
options.D: Through routine physical therapy sessions

explanation: Vectors like rodents and flies act as carriers, spreading pathogens from unsecured medical waste into surrounding residential areas. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary danger associated with genotoxic waste, such as cytotoxic cancer drugs?

options.A: It causes immediate bacterial wound infections.
options.B: It damages DNA, potentially causing mutations, birth defects, or cancer.
options.C: It emits high levels of visible light and blinding glare.
options.D: It attracts rodents and disease-carrying insects.

explanation: Genotoxic waste contains hazardous properties that alter cellular DNA, posing severe risks for mutations and cancers. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h4)

question: What environmental hazard is created when toxic medical materials are burned in open pits without proper emission controls?

options.A: Release of harmful airborne toxins like dioxins and furans
options.B: Increased oxygen production in the atmosphere
options.C: Purification of the local groundwater supply
options.D: Enhancement of soil fertility for agriculture

explanation: Open burning of medical waste releases dangerous air pollutants, including carcinogenic dioxins and furans, threatening public health. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h4)

question: Which of the following practices significantly increases the risk of a sharps injury for healthcare workers?

options.A: Using engineered safety devices
options.B: Recapping needles after patient use
options.C: Disposing of sharps immediately in puncture-proof containers
options.D: Reporting needle-stick incidents promptly

explanation: Recapping used needles is a dangerous practice that frequently leads to accidental needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h5)

question: What is the immediate priority for a nurse who sustains an accidental needle-stick injury from a used syringe?

options.A: Ignore the injury if the patient appears healthy
options.B: Hide the incident to avoid disciplinary action
options.C: Wash the wound thoroughly and follow post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) protocols
options.D: Continue the shift without reporting to save time

explanation: Prompt wound washing and adherence to PEP protocols are vital steps to minimize infection risks following a sharps injury. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h5)

question: How can improperly managed medical waste contaminate local water sources in Nigerian communities?

options.A: Through the leaching of heavy metals and pathogens into groundwater
options.B: By increasing the mineral content of bottled water factories
options.C: Through the excessive addition of medical oxygen into rivers
options.D: By purifying runoff water during heavy rainfall

explanation: Hazardous waste leaching from open dumpsites introduces harmful chemicals and pathogens into surrounding soil and groundwater tables. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h6)

question: What public health hazard is created when impoverished populations scavenge at open medical dumpsites?

options.A: Improved nutritional status and immunity
options.B: Direct exposure to infectious diseases and toxic substances
options.C: Enhanced public health awareness
options.D: Reduced incidence of chronic illnesses

explanation: Scavenging exposes individuals to direct contact with infectious waste, sharps, and hazardous chemicals, leading to severe health risks. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h6)

question: What is the standard color convention typically used for bins or bags holding infectious and anatomical waste?

options.A: Black
options.B: Yellow
options.C: Brown
options.D: White

explanation: Yellow color-coding is universally recognized for designating infectious and anatomical health care waste. [learn more](GST114_U6_T9#GST114_U6_T9_h7)

question: At what point should a waste bag or sharps container be securely closed and prepared for removal?

options.A: When it is completely overflowing and tightly packed
options.B: When it is approximately three-quarters full or reaches the fill line

question: Which Nigerian agency is involved in regulating food, drugs, and associated chemical products, contributing to health care waste guidelines?

question: What is the legal and ethical responsibility of a nurse regarding health care waste disposal guidelines?

options.A: To delegate all waste management tasks entirely to hospital administrators
options.B: To understand and comply with institutional and national regulatory standards
options.C: To create new environmental laws independent of government agencies
options.D: To dispose of hazardous waste alongside domestic trash if convenient
